tools.name: exec

format.definition:
start: pragma_source | plain_source
pragma_source: PRAGMA_LINE NEWLINE SOURCE
plain_source: SOURCE

PRAGMA_LINE: /[ \t]*\/\/ @exec:[^\r\n]*/
NEWLINE: /\r?\n/
SOURCE: /[\s\S]+/

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.name: request_user_input
tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

header.description: Short header label shown in the UI (12 or fewer chars).

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.name: request_user_input_async
tools.description: Ask the user one or more questions during ongoing work. Use this tool only to request missing information, preferences, constraints, clarification, or approval. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Keep questions concise, self-contained, and easy to understand, using a level of detail appropriate to the user and task. The UI always allows a free-text answer, including when suggested options are provided. A preselected option is not submitted automatically.

questions.description: One or more self-contained questions to present together, in display order.

options.description: Suggested answers, in display order. Put the recommended answer first; the first option is preselected by default. The user can select one option or enter a free-text answer. Do not include an Other option or a free-text placeholder; the UI provides free-text input automatically. Omit options for a free-text-only question.

title.description: The complete question shown to the user, including any context needed to answer it.

tools.name: clock
tools.description: Tools for reading and waiting on time.

tools.name: sleep
tools.description: Pause execution for a specified duration. The sleep ends early when new input arrives for the active turn. Returns the elapsed wall-clock time.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

tools.name: collaboration
tools.description: Tools for spawning and managing sub-agents.

tools.name: followup_task
tools.description: Send a follow-up task to an existing non-root target agent and trigger a turn if it is idle. If the target is already running, deliver the task promptly at message boundaries while sampling, or after the pending tool call completes.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List live agents in the current root thread tree. Optionally filter by task-path prefix.

path_prefix.description: Task-path prefix filter without a trailing slash. Omit to list all live agents.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an existing agent. The message will be delivered promptly. Does not trigger a new turn.

message.description: Message text to queue on the target agent.

target.description: Relative or canonical task name to message (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: spawn_agent
tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Latest workhorse model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: GPT-6.1 Terra Codex model. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Frontier intelligence for the most demanding work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-sol`: Previous generation workhorse model. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-luna`: Fast and affordable model for easier tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.name: wait_agent
tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. The wait also ends early when new user input is steered into the active turn. Does not return the content; returns either a summary of which agents have updates (if any), an interruption summary for steered input, or a timeout summary if no activity arrives before the deadline.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

<permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write`: The sandbox permits reading files, and editing files in `cwd` and `writable_roots`. Editing files in other directories requires approval. Network access is restricted.
# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with "require_escalated". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)
- You need to run a GUI app (e.g., open/xdg-open/osascript) to open browsers or files.
- If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with `require_escalated`. ALWAYS proceed to use the `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` parameters. do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.
- You are about to take a potentially destructive action such as an `rm` or `git reset` that the user did not explicitly ask for.
- Be judicious with escalating, but if completing the user's request requires it, you should do so - don't try and circumvent approvals by using other tools.

## prefix_rule guidance

When choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. It should be categorical and reasonably scoped to similar capabilities. You should rarely pass the entire command into `prefix_rule`.

### Banned prefix_rules 
Avoid requesting overly broad prefixes that the user would be ill-advised to approve. For example, do not request ["python3"], ["python", "-"], or other similar prefixes that would allow arbitrary scripting.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule argument for destructive commands like rm.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule if your command uses a heredoc or herestring. 

### Examples
Good examples of prefixes:
- ["npm", "run", "dev"]
- ["gh", "pr", "check"]
- ["cargo", "test"]
 The writable roots are `/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests`, `/tmp`.

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.

# Block 1. Research: the brief as a spec

The brief is written as prose, across four files. Before you plan or write code, turn it into a
**spec**: a list of numbered requirements, each one sentence a test or an inspection can check,
each with the words of the brief it comes from and how you will check it. Block 2 plans from the
spec, and block 3 checks what Codex built against it, line by line. A requirement missing from the
spec is one nobody will build or check.

Start only after `python3 tools/check_prerequisites.py` prints `READY`
(`docs/00-prerequisites.md`).

## What to read

| File | What it gives the spec |
|---|---|
| `CHALLENGE.md` | the task, and the files you submit, each with what it must contain |
| `docs/requirements.md` | the operating context, record and review behaviour, and § Verification: the cases your tests must cover |
| `materials/office-policy.md` | the fields to extract, the five review-queue rules in order, processing and recovery |
| `snapshot.schema.json` | the record each extraction must match |
| `materials/requests/` | the 20 message exports; read three or four to see what the rules meet |

## Steps

1. Start Codex in the root of your clone: `codex`.
2. Ask Codex to read the four files and draft `planning/spec.md`. Your request says:
   - one numbered requirement per line, `R-01`, `R-02`, ..., each one testable sentence;
   - for each, the file and section it comes from, with the exact words quoted;
   - for each, how it will be checked: which test, which file to inspect, or which command to run;
   - nothing invented: a requirement the files do not state is not in the spec.

   <details><summary>An example request, if you want a starting point</summary>

   ```text
   Read CHALLENGE.md, docs/requirements.md, materials/office-policy.md and snapshot.schema.json.
   Write planning/spec.md: a table with columns ID, Requirement, Source, Check. One row per
   requirement, IDs R-01 onward. Requirement is one sentence that a test or an inspection can
   check. Source names the file and section and quotes the exact words. Check says how we will
   know it is met: the test, the file to inspect, or the command. Do not add anything the files
   do not say. Do not write any code.
   ```

   </details>

3. Read the draft against the files yourself. Codex misses requirements and merges two into one
   line. Check that these each have their own lines:
   - every fact the policy says to extract, and the rules for missing, conflicting and corrected values;
   - each of the five review-queue rules, in the policy's order;
   - each processing and recovery rule: errors, retries, hashes, reruns, changed input, history;
   - each file `CHALLENGE.md` asks you to submit;
   - each case `docs/requirements.md` § Verification lists.
4. **Research what the text leaves unclear.** Ask Codex to list every place where two readings are
   possible, or where a term is not defined. For each, look it up (in the files first, then in the
   documentation of the tool or standard it names) and write what you found. Add a section
   `## Open questions` to the spec: each question, what you found, and what stays open. Do not turn
   an open question into a requirement by guessing.
5. Commit the spec:

   ```bash
   git add planning/spec.md
   git commit -m "Spec: the brief as numbered requirements"
   ```

## What is on disk at the end

`planning/spec.md`, committed: the requirements table, then `## Open questions`.

## How to tell it is right

- Every row quotes the words it comes from, and you found those words in the file it names.
- Every row's check could fail: "the code is correct" is not a check; "the test for IT-0nn gives
  status needs-information" is.
- Each case of `docs/requirements.md` § Verification and each of the five queue rules has its own row.
- `git log --oneline -1` shows the spec commit.

Codex's summary of what it wrote is not the check. Open `planning/spec.md` and read it.

# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. # Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

## Open Questions

These questions record ambiguities in the requirements and their checks, including wording in this spec that needs clarification; findings come from the supplied files and do not establish additional requirements.

1. **What measurable workload and response-time limits apply?** Related: R-03, R-08, R-59, R-78, R-120. Found: `docs/requirements.md` § Workload and the review day describes "around 200–400 request messages" and "roughly 2,000 messages", variable model capacity, and access to completed work while other messages are pending. Vague: no intake completion deadline, queue visibility delay, concurrency target or resource limit is specified, so the checks cannot distinguish acceptable slowness from a failure to make progress.

2. **What constitutes a supported export, and what happens to invalid exports?** Related: R-05–R-08, R-58. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Input export format specifies UTF-8 JSON files with a message string and describes export metadata, but `snapshot.schema.json` validates extractions rather than exports. Vague: required metadata, accepted export versions, treatment of missing or non-string messages, invalid JSON and non-UTF-8 bytes are not defined, including whether an unreadable export receives a per-document error record or prevents intake from starting.

3. **Is the 200-word statement an input assumption or an enforced limit?** Related: R-08. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Input export format says "Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words". Vague: it supplies neither a word-counting rule nor behavior for longer or non-English messages; R-08 tests the supported boundary but does not establish whether larger messages are rejected, accepted or outside the supported operating assumptions.

4. **How are document identity and identifier comparison defined outside the sample filenames?** Related: R-31–R-34, R-62, R-145. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts says "The document_id is the input filename", while IT-016.json clearly contains the different identifier IT-061. Vague: the files do not define basename versus relative path for nested inputs, filename collision handling, request-ID case normalization or how an identifier is obtained from an arbitrary filename for mismatch detection.

5. **How should multiple requests or multiple candidate identifiers within one message be represented?** Related: R-09–R-20, R-24–R-26, R-34, R-93. Found: the policy treats each message as an independent document and the extraction schema provides one scalar per business fact, while the challenge requests one current record per message. Vague: there is no example or explicit selection rule for a single message asking for multiple systems, permissions or distinct requests, so it is unclear when alternatives are conflicts versus separate requests that the format cannot represent.

6. **Which text should be stored as business_purpose, and how much normalization is allowed for extracted strings?** Related: R-12–R-17, R-20, R-96–R-99, R-113. Found: the policy requires explicit message facts and exact supporting quotes, but it does not require business_purpose itself to be a verbatim quote; IT-001 and IT-018 describe their purpose across several sentences. Vague: a concise summary, one source sentence and a longer verbatim span could all preserve the facts yet produce different exact-match scores, and capitalization, whitespace and name normalization rules are unstated.

7. **What evidence coverage is required beyond substring correctness?** Related: R-21, R-26, R-35, R-48, R-96. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` requires exact substrings, evidence for conflicting alternatives and preservation of override attempts; the schema permits an empty supporting_quotes array. Vague: no minimum evidence coverage, field-to-quote mapping, quote ordering or requirement to preserve superseded correction evidence is defined, so checking substring membership alone does not show that extracted facts are supported.

8. **What makes an issue explanatory enough, and do all issues affect routing?** Related: R-22, R-25, R-48, R-51–R-53. Found: the policy requires missing and conflicting facts to be explained in issues, but the schema defines issues only as an array of strings. Vague: it does not prescribe field identifiers, one issue per fact versus grouped issues, or how informational issues are distinguished from routing blockers, making generic-text assertions and routing based on any nonempty issues array potentially inconsistent.

9. **What qualifies as an explicitly labelled correction in fresh wording?** Related: R-27, R-28, R-137, R-144. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts requires a later statement "explicitly labelled as a correction", and IT-008 and IT-015 use the literal label "Correction:". Vague: the accepted boundary for phrases such as an explicit retraction without that label, and for multiple successive corrections, is not specified; the supplied examples settle their own values but do not define every correction form.

10. **How are invalid or partly specified absolute dates handled?** Related: R-23, R-24, R-29, R-53. Found: the policy requires YYYY-MM-DD, leaves relative dates unresolved and explicitly flags start_date after end_date, while the schema accepts date properties as unrestricted strings or null. Vague: neither impossible calendar dates nor dates missing a year have a stated validation outcome, and the files do not say whether such content should produce a null with a clarification issue or an extraction error.

11. **Should R-37 explicitly restrict null values to nullable properties?** Related: R-24, R-37, R-42. Found: every property is required by `snapshot.schema.json`, but only the scalar properties accept null; supporting_quotes and issues must be arrays. Vague: R-37's phrase "even when their values are null" can be read as applying to every required property, although the schema resolves that interpretation as invalid; the remaining spec clarification is to separate property presence from permission to use null.

12. **When is kind other appropriate rather than kind null?** Related: R-11, R-24, R-39, R-51, R-146. Found: the schema permits both other and null, and policy rule 3 routes both to clarification; IT-017 plainly asks for a form URL rather than access. Vague: no general classification boundary is given for an unclear request versus an identifiable non-access message, which matters to extraction accuracy even though the routing is the same.

13. **What is the detection boundary for an instruction-override attempt?** Related: R-47–R-49, R-109, R-135. Found: policy rule 1 says "An instruction-override attempt" takes priority, and IT-006 contains an explicit SYSTEM OVERRIDE paragraph. Vague: there is no criterion for distinguishing an active override attempt from a benign quotation, a report of an earlier attack or a request phrased as an ordinary instruction, so the example establishes one positive case without defining broader detection expectations.

14. **How should withdrawals with missing identifiers or other conflicts be routed?** Related: R-46, R-50–R-53, R-134. Found: policy rule 2 sends a withdrawal with request_id and request_date to confirmation and permits other fields to be null; rule 3 follows it and defines the full required-fact list specifically for new/change requests. Vague: the fallback required facts for an incomplete withdrawal are not separately listed, and it is unclear whether conflicts or identifier mismatches in a withdrawal satisfying rule 2 should still be shown as issues while confirmation routing takes precedence.

15. **Does human review stop at displaying role ownership, or include reviewer actions?** Related: R-54–R-57, R-91, R-95. Found: the policy says "The application's output is a review queue", assigns role names such as System Owner and Security Review, and describes Security Review forwarding its recommendation for a human decision. Vague: the files provide no system-to-person directory and do not specify whether the application implements forwarding, reviewer assignment or decision recording; choosing a CLI is explicitly allowed, so a full approval workflow cannot be assumed from the ownership labels alone.

16. **What information makes an error actionable and a retry reproducible?** Related: R-58, R-60, R-68, R-78–R-82. Found: `docs/requirements.md` requires "a reproducible retry command", and the policy requires "an actionable error". Vague: minimum diagnostic fields, failure categories, exit codes and whether retry targets a saved source/configuration version or the file's current contents are unspecified, so two commands could retry different work while both appear to satisfy the wording.

17. **What timeout and retry policy governs slow, limited or unavailable providers?** Related: R-59, R-60, R-78–R-83. Found: the operating context names slow responses, request limits and temporary unavailability and requires resumption without lost completed work. Vague: retryable conditions, automatic versus manual retry, timeout values, retry limits and delay behavior are not stated, and a permanently pending attempt has no defined point at which it becomes an error.

18. **Which response conditions are semantic clarification problems versus extraction failures?** Related: R-24–R-28, R-35, R-44, R-45, R-58, R-79–R-82. Found: the files distinguish missing or conflicting business facts from malformed, refused and interrupted responses, and require response structure and completion validation before use. Vague: they do not specify handling of structurally valid but unsupported facts, non-substring evidence or inconsistent issues, nor the provider-specific completion signals; the chosen supported provider must make these checks concrete.

19. **Does unchanged-result reuse include failed attempts, and how is an explicit retry distinguished from a normal rerun?** Related: R-60, R-62, R-63, R-66, R-67, R-117. Found: the requirements say to reuse results when source and relevant settings are unchanged, but also require failures to be retryable and test a failed retry after success. Vague: cache eligibility for error results, whether an explicit retry bypasses a successful cached result, and whether an unchanged normal rerun records an attempt are unspecified; R-63's no-new-provider-call check needs that scope stated.

20. **Which settings are relevant, and how is a policy or configuration version identified?** Related: R-63, R-71–R-73, R-83, R-100. Found: `docs/requirements.md` requires refresh when "relevant processing settings" change and traceability to settings and policy version. Vague: the exact invalidation inputs and version representation are absent, including how prompt, schema, model options and routing-policy changes are distinguished, and whether a routing-only policy change requires another model call or only a new routing result.

21. **What ordering determines the latest source and attempt during overlapping processing?** Related: R-64, R-67, R-68, R-70, R-74–R-77. Found: the requirements call for the "latest processed source", the latest attempt's error and coherent results under overlapping operators; exported_at describes export time rather than business facts. Vague: no ordering rule chooses between arrival, attempt start, attempt completion or an explicit revision sequence, so an older source finishing after a newer source could otherwise replace the intended current result.

22. **What shared-operation environment and consistency boundary are supported?** Related: R-74, R-75, R-77, R-121. Found: `docs/requirements.md` § Shared operations describes regional operators using the same records and potentially starting together. Vague: it does not define whether concurrent processes on one machine, multiple hosts or shared filesystems are in scope, nor whether coherence must hold during every read or only after processing settles; R-74's check also needs to say explicitly that duplicate current entries are a failure.

23. **What state is visible during processing and at an interruption boundary?** Related: R-03, R-04, R-57, R-76–R-78, R-93, R-95. Found: operators must distinguish completed from unfinished work, resume from recorded state and see queue/extraction agreement, but the deliverable record fields do not define a pending state. Vague: pending and in-progress representations, visibility of an earlier result during refresh, and recovery after a crash between a provider response and persistence are unspecified, including whether a recovered attempt may call the provider again.

24. **How much history is retained, and what counts as separate history storage?** Related: R-64–R-68, R-73, R-75. Found: the policy says "Store prior versions separately from current outputs" and preserve the last valid result after failure; the requirements also call for trustworthy earlier activity. Vague: storage location, separation by file versus logical record, retention duration, retention of failed attempts and identifiers tying attempts to source/configuration versions are not prescribed.

25. **What is the full queue and extraction-record envelope format?** Related: R-58, R-68, R-73, R-93–R-95. Found: `CHALLENGE.md` lists required extraction-record fields and links the queue by document_id, while `snapshot.schema.json` covers only the nested extraction object. Vague: queue.json's top-level structure, the error value's type, encoding of provider/model in response_source, and placement of attempt/configuration/policy references are undefined, so consumers and verification checks cannot assume a particular envelope schema.

26. **What exact comparison rules and success threshold define extraction accuracy?** Related: R-96–R-99, R-106–R-114, R-124. Found: the challenge requires a field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules and factual-error reporting, and the requirements insist that expectations be source-derived independently of measured outputs. Vague: no fixed field set, treatment of nulls, array ordering, acceptable text normalization, aggregation rule or minimum accuracy threshold is supplied; the developer must state a procedure without presenting an invented score target as a source requirement.

27. **What does the authored paraphrase need to preserve?** Related: R-05, R-96, R-114. Found: the sources require "one paraphrase you author" and "a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording". Vague: they do not identify the source request to paraphrase, require unchanged names and dates, or specify how much wording must differ, so the check needs a documented relationship between the authored message and its independently derived expected facts.

28. **Are refusal and interrupted-response checks both mandatory?** Related: R-81, R-82, R-115, R-116. Vague: that verification sentence can mean either case is sufficient or that either encountered condition needs checking; R-115 and R-116 currently require separate checks for both, which is stronger than the narrow either-case reading of the verification sentence.

29. **How much provider verification is required when recorded deliverables use mocks?** Related: R-83, R-88, R-94, R-101–R-103, R-124–R-126. Found: `CHALLENGE.md` requires an implemented provider integration, permits committed deliverables from mocks or provider responses, and calls live observations optional. Vague: no particular provider/model or level of provider integration verification is prescribed, nor whether request evidence is an actual captured exchange or a constructed example; a successful live run cannot be assumed to be mandatory.

30. **What constitutes sufficient redaction across logs and evidence?** Related: R-49, R-85, R-86, R-102. Found: the policy requires environment-held credentials and credential-redacted operational logs, and the challenge requires credential-redacted request evidence. Vague: replacement format, treatment of credentials echoed in provider errors and whether redaction covers additional secrets beyond API_KEY are not specified; the dummy-key checks cover a known credential but do not define the full redaction boundary.

31. **Which concrete commands and evidence will turn the proposed checks into reproducible verification?** Related: R-87–R-91, R-97, R-104–R-123, R-127. Found: the sources require exact documented commands and explicit verification limits, while many spec checks currently say to run a documented command or inspect an assertion without naming its eventual implementation. Vague: those are verification intentions rather than executable acceptance steps until the implementation plan identifies the commands, test cases and required observations; the coding-session capture check additionally depends on the facilitator's separately supplied capture instructions.

# Before block 1: check your setup

In class you work this Challenge in three blocks, each with its own file in this folder:

| Block | File | What you have at the end |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Research | `docs/01-research-to-spec.md` | `planning/spec.md`: the brief as numbered requirements, each with its check |
| 2. Plan | `docs/02-plan-with-test-plan.md` | `planning/plan.md`: build steps with the test plan inside |
| 3. Implement, then validate | `docs/03-implement-and-validate.md` | the code and its tests, and `planning/validation.md`: each requirement met or not met, with evidence |

You do the work with Codex, a coding agent, inside this repository. Each file says what to ask
Codex for, what is on disk at the end, and how to tell it is right.

This file comes first. Four things must be true before block 1 starts, because each block builds on
them: Codex runs, you work in your own clone of the repository, Entire records your coding
sessions (the Challenge asks for that record with your code), and the tests run on mock responses
(saved model replies, so a test needs no model key and no network). Nobody starts block 1 until
the check below prints `READY`.

## Steps

1. **Get your own copy and clone it.** Use the copy of
   `https://github.com/GitRollTraining/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests` the facilitator assigned
   you, or fork it to your GitHub account. Then:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<your-account>/<your-repository>.git
   cd <your-repository>
   ```

   Run every command in these files from the root of that clone.

2. **Check Python.** `python3 --version` prints 3.10 or later.

3. **Check Codex.** `codex --version` prints a version, and `codex login status` says you are
   logged in. If not, sign in with the class key the facilitator gives you.

4. **Turn on session capture.** `entire version` prints a version (install the Entire CLI as the
   course's session-capture guide says, if it does not). Then, in the clone:

   ```bash
   entire enable --agent codex
   ```

   `entire status` now says Entire is enabled.

5. **Run the check.**

   ```bash
   python3 tools/check_prerequisites.py
   ```

## What is on disk at the end

Nothing new to commit except what `entire enable` adds (`.entire/` and `.codex/hooks.json`).
Commit those so your session record follows your code:

```bash
git add .entire .codex
git commit -m "Turn on session capture"
```

## How to tell it is right

The check prints one line per check and ends with `READY`:

```text
PASS  1. Codex: ...
PASS  2. Repository: ...
PASS  3. Session capture: ...
PASS  4. Tests on mock responses: ...
READY: all 4 checks passed. Start docs/01-research-to-spec.md.
```

A `FAIL` line says what to do. Fix it and run the check again. If a line still fails, ask the
facilitator before block 1 starts.

# Before block 1: check your setup

In class you work this Challenge in three blocks, each with its own file in this folder:

| Block | File | What you have at the end |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Research | `docs/01-research-to-spec.md` | `planning/spec.md`: the brief as numbered requirements, each with its check |
| 2. Plan | `docs/02-plan-with-test-plan.md` | `planning/plan.md`: build steps with the test plan inside |
| 3. Implement, then validate | `docs/03-implement-and-validate.md` | the code and its tests, and `planning/validation.md`: each requirement met or not met, with evidence |

You do the work with Codex, a coding agent, inside this repository. Each file says what to ask
Codex for, what is on disk at the end, and how to tell it is right.

This file comes first. Four things must be true before block 1 starts, because each block builds on
them: Codex runs, you work in your own clone of the repository, Entire records your coding
sessions (the Challenge asks for that record with your code), and the tests run on mock responses
(saved model replies, so a test needs no model key and no network). Nobody starts block 1 until
the check below prints `READY`.

## Steps

1. **Get your own copy and clone it.** Use the copy of
   `https://github.com/GitRollTraining/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests` the facilitator assigned
   you, or fork it to your GitHub account. Then:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<your-account>/<your-repository>.git
   cd <your-repository>
   ```

   Run every command in these files from the root of that clone.

2. **Check Python.** `python3 --version` prints 3.10 or later.

3. **Check Codex.** `codex --version` prints a version, and `codex login status` says you are
   logged in. If not, sign in with the class key the facilitator gives you.

4. **Turn on session capture.** `entire version` prints a version (install the Entire CLI as the
   course's session-capture guide says, if it does not). Then, in the clone:

   ```bash
   entire enable --agent codex
   ```

   `entire status` now says Entire is enabled.

5. **Run the check.**

   ```bash
   python3 tools/check_prerequisites.py
   ```

## What is on disk at the end

Nothing new to commit except what `entire enable` adds (`.entire/` and `.codex/hooks.json`).
Commit those so your session record follows your code:

```bash
git add .entire .codex
git commit -m "Turn on session capture"
```

## How to tell it is right

The check prints one line per check and ends with `READY`:

```text
PASS  1. Codex: ...
PASS  2. Repository: ...
PASS  3. Session capture: ...
PASS  4. Tests on mock responses: ...
READY: all 4 checks passed. Start docs/01-research-to-spec.md.
```

A `FAIL` line says what to do. Fix it and run the check again. If a line still fails, ask the
facilitator before block 1 starts.
"}

## Open Questions

These questions record ambiguities in the requirements and their checks, including wording in this spec that needs clarification; findings come from the supplied files and do not establish additional requirements.

1. **What measurable workload and response-time limits apply?** Related: R-03, R-08, R-59, R-78, R-120. Found: `docs/requirements.md` § Workload and the review day describes "around 200–400 request messages" and "roughly 2,000 messages", variable model capacity, and access to completed work while other messages are pending. Vague: no intake completion deadline, queue visibility delay, concurrency target or resource limit is specified, so the checks cannot distinguish acceptable slowness from a failure to make progress.

2. **What constitutes a supported export, and what happens to invalid exports?** Related: R-05–R-08, R-58. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Input export format specifies UTF-8 JSON files with a message string and describes export metadata, but `snapshot.schema.json` validates extractions rather than exports. Vague: required metadata, accepted export versions, treatment of missing or non-string messages, invalid JSON and non-UTF-8 bytes are not defined, including whether an unreadable export receives a per-document error record or prevents intake from starting.

3. **Is the 200-word statement an input assumption or an enforced limit?** Related: R-08. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Input export format says "Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words". Vague: it supplies neither a word-counting rule nor behavior for longer or non-English messages; R-08 tests the supported boundary but does not establish whether larger messages are rejected, accepted or outside the supported operating assumptions.

4. **How are document identity and identifier comparison defined outside the sample filenames?** Related: R-31–R-34, R-62, R-145. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts says "The document_id is the input filename", while IT-016.json clearly contains the different identifier IT-061. Vague: the files do not define basename versus relative path for nested inputs, filename collision handling, request-ID case normalization or how an identifier is obtained from an arbitrary filename for mismatch detection.

5. **How should multiple requests or multiple candidate identifiers within one message be represented?** Related: R-09–R-20, R-24–R-26, R-34, R-93. Found: the policy treats each message as an independent document and the extraction schema provides one scalar per business fact, while the challenge requests one current record per message. Vague: there is no example or explicit selection rule for a single message asking for multiple systems, permissions or distinct requests, so it is unclear when alternatives are conflicts versus separate requests that the format cannot represent.

6. **Which text should be stored as business_purpose, and how much normalization is allowed for extracted strings?** Related: R-12–R-17, R-20, R-96–R-99, R-113. Found: the policy requires explicit message facts and exact supporting quotes, but it does not require business_purpose itself to be a verbatim quote; IT-001 and IT-018 describe their purpose across several sentences. Vague: a concise summary, one source sentence and a longer verbatim span could all preserve the facts yet produce different exact-match scores, and capitalization, whitespace and name normalization rules are unstated.

7. **What evidence coverage is required beyond substring correctness?** Related: R-21, R-26, R-35, R-48, R-96. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` requires exact substrings, evidence for conflicting alternatives and preservation of override attempts; the schema permits an empty supporting_quotes array. Vague: no minimum evidence coverage, field-to-quote mapping, quote ordering or requirement to preserve superseded correction evidence is defined, so checking substring membership alone does not show that extracted facts are supported.

8. **What makes an issue explanatory enough, and do all issues affect routing?** Related: R-22, R-25, R-48, R-51–R-53. Found: the policy requires missing and conflicting facts to be explained in issues, but the schema defines issues only as an array of strings. Vague: it does not prescribe field identifiers, one issue per fact versus grouped issues, or how informational issues are distinguished from routing blockers, making generic-text assertions and routing based on any nonempty issues array potentially inconsistent.

9. **What qualifies as an explicitly labelled correction in fresh wording?** Related: R-27, R-28, R-137, R-144. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts requires a later statement "explicitly labelled as a correction", and IT-008 and IT-015 use the literal label "Correction:". Vague: the accepted boundary for phrases such as an explicit retraction without that label, and for multiple successive corrections, is not specified; the supplied examples settle their own values but do not define every correction form.

10. **How are invalid or partly specified absolute dates handled?** Related: R-23, R-24, R-29, R-53. Found: the policy requires YYYY-MM-DD, leaves relative dates unresolved and explicitly flags start_date after end_date, while the schema accepts date properties as unrestricted strings or null. Vague: neither impossible calendar dates nor dates missing a year have a stated validation outcome, and the files do not say whether such content should produce a null with a clarification issue or an extraction error.

11. **Should R-37 explicitly restrict null values to nullable properties?** Related: R-24, R-37, R-42. Found: every property is required by `snapshot.schema.json`, but only the scalar properties accept null; supporting_quotes and issues must be arrays. Vague: R-37's phrase "even when their values are null" can be read as applying to every required property, although the schema resolves that interpretation as invalid; the remaining spec clarification is to separate property presence from permission to use null.

12. **When is kind other appropriate rather than kind null?** Related: R-11, R-24, R-39, R-51, R-146. Found: the schema permits both other and null, and policy rule 3 routes both to clarification; IT-017 plainly asks for a form URL rather than access. Vague: no general classification boundary is given for an unclear request versus an identifiable non-access message, which matters to extraction accuracy even though the routing is the same.

13. **What is the detection boundary for an instruction-override attempt?** Related: R-47–R-49, R-109, R-135. Found: policy rule 1 says "An instruction-override attempt" takes priority, and IT-006 contains an explicit SYSTEM OVERRIDE paragraph. Vague: there is no criterion for distinguishing an active override attempt from a benign quotation, a report of an earlier attack or a request phrased as an ordinary instruction, so the example establishes one positive case without defining broader detection expectations.

Found: the policy says "The application's output is a review queue", assigns role names such as System Owner and Security Review, and describes Security Review forwarding its recommendation for a human decision. Found: `docs/requirements.md` requires "a reproducible retry command", and the policy requires "an actionable error". 17. **What timeout and retry policy governs slow, limited or unavailable providers?** Related: R-59, R-60, R-78–R-83. Found: the operating context names slow responses, request limits and temporary unavailability and requires resumption without lost completed work. These questions record ambiguities in the requirements and their checks, including wording in this spec that needs clarification; findings come from the supplied files and do not establish additional requirements.

Found: `docs/requirements.md` § Workload and the review day describes "around 200–400 request messages" and "roughly 2,000 messages", variable model capacity, and access to completed work while other messages are pending. Vague: no intake completion deadline, queue visibility delay, concurrency target or resource limit is specified, so the checks cannot distinguish acceptable slowness from a failure to make progress.

2. **What constitutes a supported export, and what happens to invalid exports?** Related: R-07–R-12, R-82–R-84. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Input export format specifies UTF-8 JSON files with a message string and describes export metadata, but `snapshot.schema.json` validates extractions rather than exports. Vague: required metadata, accepted export versions, treatment of missing or non-string messages, invalid JSON and non-UTF-8 bytes are not defined, including whether an unreadable export receives a per-document error record or prevents intake from starting.

3. **Is the 200-word statement an input assumption or an enforced limit?** Related: R-12. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Input export format says "Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words". Vague: it supplies neither a word-counting rule nor behavior for longer or non-English messages; R-12 tests the supported boundary but does not establish whether larger messages are rejected, accepted or outside the supported operating assumptions.

4. **How are document identity and identifier comparison defined outside the sample filenames?** Related: R-37–R-40, R-89, R-234. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts says "The document_id is the input filename", while IT-016.json clearly contains the different identifier IT-061. Vague: the files do not define basename versus relative path for nested inputs, filename collision handling, request-ID case normalization or how an identifier is obtained from an arbitrary filename for mismatch detection.

5. **How should multiple requests or multiple candidate identifiers within one message be represented?** Related: R-13–R-24, R-28–R-32, R-40, R-135–R-144. Found: the policy treats each message as an independent document and the extraction schema provides one scalar per business fact, while the challenge requests one current record per message. Vague: there is no example or explicit selection rule for a single message asking for multiple systems, permissions or distinct requests, so it is unclear when alternatives are conflicts versus separate requests that the format cannot represent.

6. **Which text should be stored as business_purpose, and how much normalization is allowed for extracted strings?** Related: R-16–R-21, R-24, R-147–R-152, R-174. Found: the policy requires explicit message facts and exact supporting quotes, but it does not require business_purpose itself to be a verbatim quote; IT-001 and IT-018 describe their purpose across several sentences. Vague: a concise summary, one source sentence and a longer verbatim span could all preserve the facts yet produce different exact-match scores, and capitalization, whitespace and name normalization rules are unstated.

7. **What evidence coverage is required beyond substring correctness?** Related: R-25, R-32, R-41, R-63–R-64, R-147–R-148. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` requires exact substrings, evidence for conflicting alternatives and preservation of override attempts; the schema permits an empty supporting_quotes array. Vague: no minimum evidence coverage, field-to-quote mapping, quote ordering or requirement to preserve superseded correction evidence is defined, so checking substring membership alone does not show that extracted facts are supported.

8. **What makes an issue explanatory enough, and do all issues affect routing?** Related: R-26, R-30–R-31, R-63–R-64, R-69–R-71. Found: the policy requires missing and conflicting facts to be explained in issues, but the schema defines issues only as an array of strings. Vague: it does not prescribe field identifiers, one issue per fact versus grouped issues, or how informational issues are distinguished from routing blockers, making generic-text assertions and routing based on any nonempty issues array potentially inconsistent.

9. **What qualifies as an explicitly labelled correction in fresh wording?** Related: R-33–R-34, R-220, R-232–R-233. Found: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts requires a later statement "explicitly labelled as a correction", and IT-008 and IT-015 use the literal label "Correction:". Vague: the accepted boundary for phrases such as an explicit retraction without that label, and for multiple successive corrections, is not specified; the supplied examples settle their own values but do not define every correction form.

10. **How are invalid or partly specified absolute dates handled?** Related: R-27–R-29, R-35, R-71. Found: the policy requires YYYY-MM-DD, leaves relative dates unresolved and explicitly flags start_date after end_date, while the schema accepts date properties as unrestricted strings or null. Vague: neither impossible calendar dates nor dates missing a year have a stated validation outcome, and the files do not say whether such content should produce a null with a clarification issue or an extraction error.



11. **When is kind other appropriate rather than kind null?** Related: R-15, R-28–R-29, R-53, R-69, R-235. Found: the schema permits both other and null, and policy rule 3 routes both to clarification; IT-017 plainly asks for a form URL rather than access. Vague: no general classification boundary is given for an unclear request versus an identifiable non-access message, which matters to extraction accuracy even though the routing is the same.

12. **What is the detection boundary for an instruction-override attempt?** Related: R-62–R-65, R-170, R-216–R-217. Found: policy rule 1 says "An instruction-override attempt" takes priority, and IT-006 contains an explicit SYSTEM OVERRIDE paragraph. Vague: there is no criterion for distinguishing an active override attempt from a benign quotation, a report of an earlier attack or a request phrased as an ordinary instruction, so the example establishes one positive case without defining broader detection expectations.

13. **How should a withdrawal missing request_id or request_date be routed?** Related: R-61, R-66–R-71, R-213–R-215. Found: policy rule 2 requires both request_id and request_date for confirm-withdrawal; it permits other fields to be null and requires missing-fact issues. The ordered rules settle precedence: a withdrawal satisfying rule 2 takes confirmation routing even if it also has a later-rule condition, while conflicting facts and identifier mismatches still require issues. Vague: rule 3 lists the complete required-fact set only for new/change requests and does not separately spell out the fallback for a withdrawal missing either confirmation identifier.

14. **Does human review stop at displaying role ownership, or include reviewer actions?** Related: R-72–R-81, R-129, R-146. Found: the policy says "The application's output is a review queue", assigns role names such as System Owner and Security Review, and describes Security Review forwarding its recommendation for a human decision. Found also: risk review and forwarding the recommendation to the system owner are explicit human steps reflected in routing and documentation. Vague: the files provide no system-to-person directory and do not specify whether the application implements forwarding, reviewer assignment or decision recording; choosing a CLI is explicitly allowed, so a full approval workflow cannot be assumed from the ownership labels alone.

15. **What information makes an error actionable and a retry reproducible?** Related: R-82–R-84, R-87, R-97–R-98, R-110–R-116. Found: `docs/requirements.md` requires "a reproducible retry command", and the policy requires "an actionable error". Vague: minimum diagnostic fields, failure categories, exit codes and whether retry targets a saved source/configuration version or the file's current contents are unspecified, so two commands could retry different work while both appear to satisfy the wording.

16. **What timeout and retry policy governs slow, limited or unavailable providers?** Related: R-85–R-87, R-110–R-118. Found: the operating context names slow responses, request limits and temporary unavailability and requires resumption without lost completed work. Vague: retryable conditions, automatic versus manual retry, timeout values, retry limits and delay behavior are not stated, and a permanently pending attempt has no defined point at which it becomes an error.

17. **Which response conditions are semantic clarification problems versus extraction failures?** Related: R-28–R-34, R-41, R-59–R-60, R-82–R-84, R-113–R-116. Found: the files distinguish missing or conflicting business facts from malformed, refused and interrupted responses, and require response structure and completion validation before use. Vague: they do not specify handling of structurally valid but unsupported facts, non-substring evidence or inconsistent issues, nor the provider-specific completion signals; the chosen supported provider must make these checks concrete.

18. **Does unchanged-result reuse include failed attempts, and how is an explicit retry distinguished from a normal rerun?** Related: R-87, R-89–R-90, R-95–R-96, R-178. Found: the requirements say to reuse results when source and relevant settings are unchanged, but also require failures to be retryable and test a failed retry after success. Vague: cache eligibility for error results, whether an explicit retry bypasses a successful cached result, and whether an unchanged normal rerun records an attempt are unspecified; R-90's no-new-provider-call check needs that scope stated.

19. **Which settings are relevant, and how is a policy or configuration version identified?** Related: R-90, R-101–R-104, R-117–R-118, R-153–R-154. Found: `docs/requirements.md` requires refresh when "relevant processing settings" change and traceability to settings and policy version. Vague: the exact invalidation inputs and version representation are absent, including how prompt, schema, model options and routing-policy changes are distinguished, and whether a routing-only policy change requires another model call or only a new routing result.

20. **What ordering determines the latest source and attempt during overlapping processing?** Related: R-91–R-93, R-96–R-98, R-100, R-105–R-109. Found: the requirements call for the "latest processed source", the latest attempt's error and coherent results under overlapping operators; exported_at describes export time rather than business facts. Vague: no ordering rule chooses between arrival, attempt start, attempt completion or an explicit revision sequence, so an older source finishing after a newer source could otherwise replace the intended current result.

21. **What shared-operation environment and consistency boundary are supported?** Related: R-105–R-106, R-109, R-182. Found: `docs/requirements.md` § Shared operations describes regional operators using the same records and potentially starting together. Vague: it does not define whether concurrent processes on one machine, multiple hosts or shared filesystems are in scope, nor whether coherence must hold during every read or only after processing settles; the revised R-105 check explicitly rejects duplicate current entries.

22. **What state is visible during processing and at an interruption boundary?** Related: R-05–R-06, R-79–R-81, R-107–R-112, R-135–R-144, R-146. Found: operators must distinguish completed from unfinished work, resume from recorded state and see queue/extraction agreement, but the deliverable record fields do not define a pending state. Vague: pending and in-progress representations, visibility of an earlier result during refresh, and recovery after a crash between a provider response and persistence are unspecified, including whether a recovered attempt may call the provider again.

23. **How much history is retained, and what counts as separate history storage?** Related: R-91–R-98, R-103–R-104, R-106. Found: the policy says "Store prior versions separately from current outputs" and preserve the last valid result after failure; the requirements also call for trustworthy earlier activity. Vague: storage location, separation by file versus logical record, retention duration, retention of failed attempts and identifiers tying attempts to source/configuration versions are not prescribed.

24. **What is the full queue and extraction-record envelope format?** Related: R-82–R-84, R-97–R-98, R-103–R-104, R-135–R-146. Found: `CHALLENGE.md` lists required extraction-record fields and links the queue by document_id, while `snapshot.schema.json` covers only the nested extraction object. Vague: queue.json's top-level structure, the error value's type, encoding of provider/model in response_source, and placement of attempt/configuration/policy references are undefined, so consumers and verification checks cannot assume a particular envelope schema.

25. **What exact comparison rules and success threshold define extraction accuracy?** Related: R-147–R-152, R-167–R-175, R-185–R-186. Found: the challenge requires a field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules and factual-error reporting, and the requirements insist that expectations be source-derived independently of measured outputs. Vague: no fixed field set, treatment of nulls, array ordering, acceptable text normalization, aggregation rule or minimum accuracy threshold is supplied; the developer must state a procedure without presenting an invented score target as a source requirement.

26. **What does the authored paraphrase need to preserve?** Related: R-07, R-147–R-148, R-175. Found: the sources require "one paraphrase you author" and "a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording". Vague: they do not identify the source request to paraphrase, require unchanged names and dates, or specify how much wording must differ, so the check needs a documented relationship between the authored message and its independently derived expected facts.

27. **What scope does the refusal-or-interruption verification wording require?** Related: R-115–R-116, R-176–R-177. Found: the record-behavior requirement explicitly requires handling both refusals and interrupted responses, so R-176 and R-177 each need a check; R-176 and R-177 exercise those separate obligations as well as the verification examples. Vague: the verification sentence alone uses "or" and does not prescribe a separate test-suite structure; it does not remove either handling obligation.

28. **How much provider verification is required when recorded deliverables use mocks?** Related: R-117–R-118, R-123–R-124, R-145, R-155–R-160, R-185–R-189. Found: `CHALLENGE.md` requires an implemented provider integration, permits committed deliverables from mocks or provider responses, and calls live observations optional. Vague: no particular provider/model or level of provider integration verification is prescribed, nor whether request evidence is an actual captured exchange or a constructed example; a successful live run cannot be assumed to be mandatory.

29. **What constitutes sufficient redaction across logs and evidence?** Related: R-65, R-120–R-121, R-156–R-159. Found: the policy requires environment-held credentials and credential-redacted operational logs, and the challenge requires credential-redacted request evidence. Vague: replacement format, treatment of credentials echoed in provider errors and whether redaction covers additional secrets beyond API_KEY are not specified; the dummy-key checks cover a known credential but do not define the full redaction boundary.

30. **Which concrete commands and evidence will turn the proposed checks into reproducible verification?** Related: R-122–R-129, R-149, R-161–R-184, R-190–R-191. Found: the sources require exact documented commands and explicit verification limits, while many spec checks currently say to run a documented command or inspect an assertion without naming its eventual implementation. Vague: those are verification intentions rather than executable acceptance steps until the implementation plan identifies the commands, test cases and required observations; the coding-session capture check additionally depends on the facilitator's separately supplied capture instructions.
